title: Metrics Monitoring and Alerting
summary: Design a monitoring platform that collects metrics, stores time series, and triggers reliable alerts.
statement: Design a metrics monitoring system like Prometheus or Datadog. It collects metrics from thousands of services, stores time series efficiently, serves dashboard queries, and evaluates alert rules with low delay. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Query with aggregation over time ranges.

requirementQuestions.question: How many series and data points per second?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: How fresh must dashboards and alerts be?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: Must alerting keep working when the monitored system or the monitor partly fails?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: What retention and resolution are required?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Pull or push collection, and which cardinality limits apply?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: How is storage cost controlled for high-cardinality labels?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Prevents over-engineering and affects build-versus-buy choices.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How much storage per day at 2 bytes per compressed point?
How many alert evaluations per second?
How much memory does the series index need?

keyDecisions.question: How are metrics gathered?
considerations: Pull scraping gives control and discovery; push suits short-lived jobs.

keyDecisions.question: How are points stored?
considerations: Append-optimised store with delta compression and blocks by time.
Series index maps labels to series IDs.

keyDecisions.question: How are queries executed?
considerations: Fan out to shards and merge aggregates.

keyDecisions.question: How are alerts evaluated reliably?
considerations: A dedicated evaluator reads recent data on a schedule.
Alert on missing data and on the monitor itself.

keyDecisions.question: How is growth controlled?
considerations: Downsample old data to coarser resolution.
Tier cold data to cheaper storage.

tradeoffs.tension: Control and simplicity versus handling ephemeral workloads.

commonMistakes: Using a general relational database for time series.
Alerting that depends on the failing system alone.
followUps: How do you make alerting highly available?
How do you handle a cardinality explosion?
How do you support multi-tenant isolation?
How do you detect anomalies without static thresholds?
